newsitem.title: USA: NY Fed McDonough sees electronic money a challenge.
newsitem.headline: NY Fed McDonough sees electronic money a challenge.

text.p: Federal Reserve Bank of New York President William McDonough said on Tuesday new technology poses a challenge to the banking system and to central banks.

"Retail banking is going through an electronic transformation. The only questions are how far and how fast this transformation will take place," McDonough told a banking conference on the National Payment System here.
"Electronic money has become an important issue not only for the Federal Reserve, but for central banks around the world," he added.

McDonough, who also chairs the Group of Ten committee on payment and settlements systems, said, "To fulfill our monetary policy responsibilities as well as our roles in operating and overseeing payment systems, central banks need to understand the effects of changes in the form of money and the way it is transmitted."
McDonough said the G-10 central banks need to monitor and share information -- mainly regarding the issue of security.
"I believe our focus on the need to fully understand, continuously monitor and share information internationally on electronic money is the appropriate one," he said.
McDonough then turned to another issue raised by the development of electronic money -- whether non-banks will become major issuers.

"The private sector appears to be developing the technology and the networks that should eventually allow electronic money to circulate at par across the nation... with adequate effectiveness, scope and equity," the New York Fed president said. "There does not appear to be a case for the Federal Reserve to issue electronic money at this time," he added.
McDonough next addressed another form of payment system that may also soon develop on the Internet.

"Some efforts are underway to adapt electronic money so that it could flow... securely over an open computer network," said McDonough, noting the possible threat computers hackers may pose and the challenge to traditional banking services.
"Banks could lose control over the distribution network as we move toward virtual commerce," McDonough added. "In this case, banking products might become like commodities."
But McDonough said this would not mean the end of bank branches, but rather their evolution into "one-stop financial service centers."
Finally, McDonough discussed the role the Fed plays in developing electronic check clearing with commercial banks as well as other financial services innovations.
"Banks, as well as bank supervisors, will need to think carefully about all the potential implications of this new paradigm for retail banking," he concluded.
